extracted.intended_audience: general public; students; researchers; consumer advocates; policymakers interested in consumer finance and mortgage lending
extracted.subtask_description: Identify, describe, and evaluate practices and legal/regulatory indicators that constitute predatory lending, including loan terms, disclosures, servicing behavior, and targeting of vulnerable groups. Covers definitions, common abusive practices, underlying causes, and relevant U.S. legislation and guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: FDIC OIG definition of predatory lending
rubrics_metrics.description: "Imposing unfair and abusive loan terms on borrowers" (FDIC OIG, 2006)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes there is no internationally agreed legal definition; FDIC OIG's phrasing is used as a broad operational definition. 'Unfair' and 'abusive' are not specifically defined in that report; the term is used as a catch-all for multiple specific illegal or unethical loan-industry activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral-backed loan vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Predatory lending typically occurs on loans backed by collateral (e.g., car or house) so that repossession or foreclosure can be used to profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lenders may structure loans or mislead borrowers about terms or ability to pay so that default (and subsequent repossession/foreclosure and resale) generates profit for the lender or their agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unjustified risk-based pricing
rubrics_metrics.description: Charging higher interest rates and fees for borrowers identified as greater credit risks (risk-based pricing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lenders argue this is legitimate to offset higher default risk; consumer groups argue higher prices paid by vulnerable consumers are not always justified and can be used as an excuse to overcharge. The topic is controversial and central to debates over what is 'predatory.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-premium credit insurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Selling a single-premium credit insurance product rolled into the loan that pays off the loan if the borrower dies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This insurance is usually more expensive than alternatives, customers often are not shown choices (lender may be unlicensed to sell alternatives), and the cost is financed into the loan, raising the loan's overall cost while masking upfront payment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to present loan price as negotiable
rubrics_metrics.description: Not informing borrowers that aspects of loan pricing and terms are negotiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many borrowers — especially unsophisticated ones — may not know they can negotiate interest rates or charges and may assume the lender's offer is fixed, causing them to accept worse terms than they might obtain if they negotiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to clearly and accurately disclose terms and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inadequate or misleading disclosure of loan terms and conditions, particularly when borrowers are unsophisticated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mortgage transactions involve complex documents and multiple parties; in the most egregious cases lenders or brokers have misled borrowers or altered documents after signing. Clear, accurate disclosure is a core protective standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-term loans with disproportionately high fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Products (e.g., payday loans, tax refund anticipation loans, certain credit card late fees, overdraft fees) where fees for short-term advances equate to extremely high annualized interest rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originators often dispute calling these fees 'interest.' Consumer advocates treat such pricing as predatory when the annualized cost far exceeds market rates for high-risk loans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Servicing-agent and securitization abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Abuses related to the mortgage servicing agent and securitization process, including changes in servicer, failures to forward payments, and the loan being traded without borrower consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal law requires notice when servicing agents change, but borrowers can still be held delinquent if payments go to an agent who fails to forward them. Trading of notes and difficulty locating original notes can lead to wrongful foreclosure or eviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreclosure and eviction without proper notice or defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreclosures carried out without proper notice, and in some jurisdictions eviction can proceed without a defense (example: Texas Rule of Civil Procedure 746).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems include inability of claimed note owners to produce original notes, reliance on affidavits rather than proving 'holder in due course,' and borrowers being forced to incur litigation and relocation costs while contesting ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loan flipping
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent refinancings that provide little or no economic benefit to the borrower but generate fees, prepayment penalties, and additional charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified in OCC Advisory Letter AL 2003-2; flip-refinancings are undertaken primarily to generate fees rather than to help borrowers, and are a classic predatory pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinancing to strip subsidized benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Refinancings of special subsidized mortgages that result in loss of beneficial loan terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowers may be induced into refinancing and thereby lose government-subsidized or other favorable terms, increasing their long-term costs or risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Packing" excessive or hidden fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Including excessive or hidden fees in the amount financed (fee 'packing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees embedded in the financed amount increase loan cost without borrowers' clear awareness; this is frequently cited as an abusive practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of loan structures like negative amortization
rubrics_metrics.description: Using terms or structures (e.g., negative amortization) that make it harder or impossible for borrowers to reduce or repay indebtedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such structures can defer principal increases or hide true repayment burden, leading borrowers into deeper debt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of balloon payments to conceal burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Using balloon payments to hide the true burden of financing and to force borrowers into costly refinancing or foreclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balloon payments can produce deceptively low periodic payments and then a large lump-sum obligation, pressuring borrowers into further risky transactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting vulnerable borrowers with inappropriate products
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketing or steering older borrowers, the financially unsophisticated, or borrowers who could qualify for mainstream credit into inappropriate or excessively expensive credit products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeting based on vulnerability or past exclusion from mainstream credit is frequently cited as predatory; regulators treat steering vulnerable groups into high-cost products as abusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadequate disclosure of costs, risks, and appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to adequately disclose the true costs, risks, and whether a loan is appropriate for the borrower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond basic term disclosure, lenders should ensure borrowers understand affordability and risk; failure to do so is an OCC-identified predatory indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory arbitration clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of mandatory arbitration clauses that limit borrowers' ability to pursue court remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandatory arbitration can be used to shield lenders from class actions and public scrutiny; regulators consider their use in consumer contracts a potential abusive practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting of minority and disadvantaged communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Predatory lending disproportionately made in poor and minority neighborhoods and sometimes resulting in mortgage discrimination based on race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations and studies cited (ACORN, HUD, ACLU, etc.) show higher prevalence of subprime and predatory loans in minority communities; even with comparable incomes minorities were more likely to get subprime loans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcharging and excessive fee levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Charging fees or rates well above typical averages (page cites examples: average fee should be ~1% but predatory lenders charged over 5%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High fee percentages (relative to norms) are a quantitative signal of predation; critics argue such levels drove parts of the subprime crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting other vulnerable groups (e.g., women, first-time buyers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Steering women and first-time home buyers — who may lack financial experience — into subprime or otherwise unfavorable loan products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly and media reports identified women and first-time buyers as groups especially vulnerable to aggressive sales tactics and unsuitable loans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media-documented abusive sales tactics (e.g., 'boiler room' practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of bait-and-switch salesmanship, forgery, falsified appraisals, and fabricating income to qualify borrowers (example: Ameriquest scandal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative reporting and legal settlements show how aggressive sales operations and fraud can be part of predatory lending schemes; large settlements (e.g., Ameriquest) are cited as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dispute about labeling and availability effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that some practices labeled 'predatory' (notably risk-based pricing) are legitimate and that anti-predatory laws can reduce credit availability for low-income borrowers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some industry groups view 'predatory lending' as a pejorative; empirical results on the effects of anti-predatory laws are mixed and can include unintended increases in high-cost mortgage applications in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial practice and burden of proof issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Court practices that tend to favor lenders and shift burdens to borrowers (e.g., requiring borrowers to prove payments reached the note owner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When courts allow affidavits instead of original-note proof or do not treat lender-borrower relationship as fiduciary, borrowers face higher hurdles to defend against foreclosure or collection claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition as mitigating or insufficient force
rubrics_metrics.description: View that competition between lenders should prevent overcharging versus evidence that competition may not protect uninformed consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents argue markets curb excess; critics point to information asymmetry and market segments where competition doesn't reduce abusive pricing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial education and counseling interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers' lack of understanding of APR and time value can make them vulnerable; counseling mandates can change borrower choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A legislative experiment requiring offers be reviewed by HUD-certified counselors in some Illinois zip codes showed borrowers chose less risky products to avoid counseling, indicating counseling can influence outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat emptor and absence of lender fiduciary duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The legal principle that borrowers must look out for themselves; most U.S. courts refuse to treat the lender-borrower relationship as fiduciary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a result, when statutory disclosures are made, courts often place responsibility on borrowers to determine loan suitability; this legal backdrop affects which practices are regulated versus left to market choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predatory borrowing and fraud by applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Borrower-side fraud and misrepresentations (e.g., overstated income, falsified documents) that contributed to defaults and complicate the predatory-lending narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies cited show a large share of early payment defaults involved misrepresentations; the page notes brokers or loan officers sometimes created or facilitated falsified applications; distinction between predatory lending and borrower fraud is discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predatory servicing (post-origination abuses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unfair, deceptive or fraudulent practices by loan servicers after loan origination, including charging excessive/unsubstantiated servicing fees, wrongful default reporting, borrower harassment, and refusal to act in good faith on required mortgage modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predatory servicing is treated as a component of predatory lending; it includes improper fees and bad-faith conduct that can lead to foreclosure despite borrower efforts to comply or modify loans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and regulatory protections (TILA, HOEPA, state laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence of federal (Truth in Lending Act, Section 32 / HOEPA) and state anti-predatory laws that define 'high-cost' or 'covered' loans and impose additional restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While TILA requires APR and term disclosures, HOEPA targets certain high-cost mortgage features; many states have their own laws that trigger extra restrictions or penalties for 'covered' loans based on fees or APR thresholds.
